name: Fatima Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the livestock lead at Greenhollow, a co-operative farm owned by about forty members, me included with one small share. We've 70 dairy cows, a bit of wheat and oats, and a farm shop that sells our milk and yoghurt. I'm in the parlour by half five, then calves, then feed planning, then whatever meeting the co-op has dreamed up that week. I love the calves. I could do without the meetings, though I'd defend them to anyone.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Being the person in between. The board wants costs down, the younger members want everything organic, and the cows just want to be milked on time. My partner Sam works at the council roads depot, and our two, Yusuf and Mira, are eleven and eight. I do use one of those AI chat tools now and then, mostly to tidy up grant forms, because I hate writing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. Some of the board would be disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can stop talking about it and get on with milking. Half our meetings last year were about whether to buy a robot milker. I'd post something cheerful in the co-op group chat, probably a picture of a cow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me fine. My job's safe, our members keep their say, and I keep using the chat tool for grant forms, which saves me maybe two evenings a quarter. The things that actually worry me, milk prices and feed costs, are the same as ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am. I'd probably push the co-op to spend the robot milker money on a new calf shed instead, about 40,000 we'd been setting aside. At home we'd keep putting 200 a month into savings like we already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little flat, maybe, because I'd got used to the idea of something big coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with those two evenings the AI saves you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the two evenings the AI saves me, I'd sit at my daughter Mira's swimming lessons without a laptop on my knee. That sounds small, but it's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the co-op who'd be disappointed it fizzled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, our youngest member, would be gutted. He's been reading about robot weeders for two years and he'd have to find a new hobby. I'd buy him a pint and tell him the calf shed is exciting too.

S0.say: Good, now we can stop talking about it and get on with milking. Half our meetings last year were about whether to buy a robot milker.
S0.think: It suits me fine: my job's safe and our members keep their say. The things that really worry me, milk prices and feed costs, stay the same.
S0.do: Keeps going as she is and pushes the co-op to spend the robot milker fund, about 40,000, on a new calf shed. Keeps saving 200 a month at home.
S0.feel: Calm, and slightly flat after expecting something big.
S0.quote: With the two evenings the AI saves me, I'd sit at my daughter Mira's swimming lessons without a laptop on my knee.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima sees the co-op's structure as a buffer, and expects her real worries to stay economic. She uses AI modestly and values the time it saves for family. She already thinks in terms of what the co-op should vote for.

steps.text: Push the co-op to spend the 40,000 robot milker fund on a new calf shed
Keep milking the 70 cows and using the chat tool for grant forms
Keep putting 200 a month into the family savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd bet on, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to make sure the co-op decides how the robots come in, not the machinery dealer. I'd say it to the members and probably on the farmers' forum. Change is fine if the people doing the work have a vote on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes more than it disappears. A robot milker would take my mornings, but someone still has to know when a cow's off her feed. I'd go from milking to managing data and health, and I'm not sure I'd like that as much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until two or three farms near us have had robot milkers running for a year, then back the co-op buying one. I'd go on the dealer's two-day training and learn the herd software properly. And I'd ask the union to negotiate what happens to the two part-time milkers we employ.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can manage. It's change, not loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to those two part-time milkers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me awake in this one. Grace has worked with us for nine years and she's 58, so she's not going to retrain into software. I'd fight for the co-op to keep her on for calf work, even if it costs us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure you'd like the job as much. What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The warmth, honestly. Nothing beats standing between two cows on a January morning with your hands on a warm flank. You don't get that from a screen showing yield graphs.

S1.say: The co-op should decide how robots come in, not the machinery dealer. Change is fine if the people doing the work have a vote on it.
S1.think: My job changes more than it disappears: a robot milker takes my mornings, but someone still has to know when a cow is off her feed. I'm not sure I'd enjoy the data side as much.
S1.do: Waits until nearby farms have run robot milkers for a year, then backs the co-op buying one and does the dealer's two-day training. Asks the union to negotiate the future of the two part-time milkers.
S1.feel: Uneasy but manageable, more change than loss.
S1.quote: Nothing beats standing between two cows on a January morning with your hands on a warm flank. You don't get that from a screen showing yield graphs.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima is a classic 'once it's proven' adopter and puts her trust in co-op votes and union deals. Her strongest worry was for Grace, a 58-year-old colleague, not herself. She expects to miss the physical warmth of the work.

steps.text: Wait until two or three nearby farms have run robot milkers for a year
Take the dealer's two-day training and learn the herd software properly
Ask the union to negotiate the future of the co-op's two part-time milkers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's not long enough for the co-op to even finish a vote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what public support is for. If AI can do every job, then the profits from it have to be shared, through taxes or a basic income, or we're all in trouble. I'd say it loudly, at the co-op, at the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the co-op would be bought out or undercut within a year. Big robot dairies would sell milk cheaper than we can produce it, and our members would vote to sell rather than go bankrupt. I'd lose my job and my small share would be worth less than a used car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month we'd stop the 200 a month into savings and put it towards the mortgage instead, to shorten it. We'd cancel the new kitchen we'd planned for next spring. I'd join every campaign for a shared AI dividend, and I'd apply for whatever retraining grant appeared the day it appeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: None if I can help it, but the car would go before the mortgage. Sam's job at the depot might last a bit longer, since roads still need patching, so we'd live on his wage and our savings for maybe four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yusuf and Mira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the cows are going to a new farm and Mum's going to find a new job. My son Yusuf would ask if the robots are nice to the cows. I genuinely wouldn't know what to tell him.

S2.say: This is exactly what public support is for. If AI can do every job, the profits have to be shared through taxes or a basic income.
S2.think: The co-op would be bought out or undercut by big robot dairies within a year. I'd lose my job, and my small share would be worth less than a used car.
S2.do: Stops monthly saving and pays the money into the mortgage, and cancels next spring's new kitchen. Joins campaigns for a shared AI dividend and applies for retraining grants the day they appear.
S2.quote: My son Yusuf would ask if the robots are nice to the cows. I genuinely wouldn't know what to tell him.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI breaks Fatima's faith that the co-op can manage change through votes. She expects members to sell rather than fight a losing price war. Her answer is political, a shared dividend, alongside careful household budgeting around her partner's job.

steps.text: Cancel the new kitchen planned for next spring
Switch the 200 a month savings to paying down the mortgage faster
Campaign at the co-op, the union and online for a shared AI dividend
Apply for any retraining grant on the day it opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's enough time to see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farms like ours need help to buy in together, so we're not wiped out by the big players. I'd push for public grants for co-ops to share robots and keep people on. I'd say it at the regional co-op federation, which I've never spoken at before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the co-op survives in a smaller form, maybe as a shop and a showcase farm with robots doing the milking. There'd be room for one or two people like me who know the animals. Whether that's me or Jonah depends on who learns faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the robot maintenance and herd health course at the agricultural college within the first year, evenings, about 900 for the year. I'd keep the savings at 200 a month and add the farm shop's Saturday shift for an extra 80 a week. And I'd want the co-op to buy its first robots in year two, not year five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do about it. That's a big difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years you said you'd lose your job. What does five change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to be the one who runs the robots instead of the one they replace. In two years nobody's trained and nobody's ready. In five, I could be the person the co-op can't do without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Jonah. Would you be competing with him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, and I don't love that. He's 26 and he lives on his phone. But I know the herd, I know which cow kicks, and I think the co-op would want both of us if I argue for it properly.

S3.say: Farms like ours need help to buy in together so we're not wiped out by the big players. There should be public grants for co-ops to share robots and keep people on.
S3.think: The co-op survives smaller, maybe as a shop and showcase farm with robots doing the milking. There'd be room for one or two people who know the animals, and it depends who learns faster.
S3.do: Enrols in an evening robot maintenance and herd health course at the agricultural college, about 900 for the year. Keeps saving 200 a month, takes an extra Saturday shift at the farm shop, and pushes the co-op to buy robots in year two.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with something useful to do about it.
S3.quote: Five years gives me time to be the one who runs the robots instead of the one they replace.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Fatima moves from protest to positioning herself. She'd retrain, push the co-op to adopt early and argue for public grants for co-ops. She admits some discomfort at competing with a younger colleague.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's evening robot maintenance and herd health course, about 900
Keep saving 200 a month into the family savings
Take the farm shop's Saturday shift for an extra 80 a week
Speak at the regional co-op federation for public grants to share robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Yusuf would be 21.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got no excuse not to do this well. Ten years is enough for proper rules on who owns the machines, retraining for everyone and a fair share of the money. I'd be helping the co-op federation write a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm much calmer about this one. I'd retrain at my own pace, see which robots actually work on farms like ours, and probably end up doing something with animal health that a robot can't fully do yet. I'd be 53, and I think I'd still be useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first couple of years I'd do the herd health course, then wait and watch the robot milkers on other farms before backing one. I'd start a small education fund for the kids, 40 a month each. And I'd join the federation's policy group and go to the open meetings with our representative.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. It feels like something that could go right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell the kids anything different about their future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I'd tell them not to bet everything on one job, because I did and it worked out but they might not be so lucky. Mira likes drawing and animals, and I'd tell her to keep both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about ten years that worries you more than five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people would get lazy. With ten years, the board would keep saying we'll deal with it next year. Ten years just makes people lazy, and I've seen the co-op board put off a new calf shed for six years running.

S4.say: We've got no excuse not to do this well. Ten years is enough for proper rules on who owns the machines, retraining for everyone and a fair share of the money.
S4.think: I'm much calmer about this one. I'd retrain at my own pace, see which robots work on farms like ours, and probably end up in animal health work a robot can't fully do yet.
S4.do: Takes the herd health course in the first couple of years and waits to see robot milkers proven elsewhere before backing one. Starts education funds of 40 a month for each child and joins the co-op federation's policy group.
S4.quote: Ten years just makes people lazy, and I've seen the co-op board put off a new calf shed for six years running.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns Fatima hopeful and methodical. Her new worry is complacency on the co-op board rather than the technology. She'd advise her children to spread their bets across more than one kind of work.

steps.text: Take the herd health course in the first couple of years
Watch robot milkers on other farms before backing one for Greenhollow
Start education funds of 40 a month each for Yusuf and Mira
Join the co-op federation's policy group and the representative's open meetings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the co-op couldn't move fast enough and we'd be undercut before anyone voted on anything. What would help is public money for co-ops to buy robots together and keep their people, and a basic income while families like ours adjust.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked what happens to the animals. Everyone talks about jobs. But a cow that's been handled by the same person for years notices when that person's gone.

headlineQuote: A cow that's been handled by the same person for years notices when that person's gone.
portrait: Fatima Walsh, 43, is livestock lead at Greenhollow, a members' co-operative dairy, and holds one small share. She uses an AI chat tool now and then for grant forms and trusts co-op votes and union deals to steer change. She's calm if AI stalls and uneasy with steady change, mostly worrying for an older colleague. Fast AGI alarms her because she expects big robot dairies to undercut the co-op; with five or ten years she would retrain in herd health and robot maintenance and push for public grants.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the co-op couldn't move fast enough and would be undercut before it could even vote.
whatWouldHelp: Public money for co-ops to buy robots together and keep their workers, plus a basic income while families adjust.
